title: Minerals: Building Blocks of Rocks
summary: What minerals are, and how scientists use properties like hardness, luster, and streak to tell different minerals apart.
poll: Two minerals that look the same color must be the same mineral.

versions.title: What Is a Mineral?
versions.text:
Look at a rock. You may see many tiny bits in it. We call these bits minerals. A mineral is hard. It is not alive. It comes from the ground.

Each one has its own look. Some are shiny. Some are dull. Some are hard. Some are soft. You can test how hard one is. Try to scratch it with a nail. Try a coin too. A hard one will not get a scratch.

These bits grow in neat shapes. We call the shapes crystals. A crystal has flat sides.

One common kind is quartz. It is very hard. It is often clear or white. Another kind is halite. We call it rock salt. We eat it every day. A soft kind called gypsum is used to make chalk.

People who dig in the desert find useful bits like this. They find salt, gold, and other rocks. They are all around us. We even use them at home.

Look closely at a rock. You will see many tiny bits in it. We call these bits minerals. A mineral is hard. It does not live. It comes from the ground.

Each one has its own look. Some are very shiny. Some look dull. Some are quite hard. Some are much softer. One way to test hardness is to scratch it with a nail or a coin. A hard one will resist a scratch. A soft one will show a mark.

These bits often grow in neat shapes called crystals. These shapes have flat, straight sides.

One very common kind is quartz. It is very hard. It is often clear, white, or pink. Another kind, halite, is better known as rock salt. People eat it every day. A much softer kind called gypsum is used to make chalk and plaster.

People who dig in the desert find useful bits like salt, gold, and other rocks. These bits truly are all around us, even inside things we use at home.

versions.title: What Are Minerals?
versions.text:
Look closely at almost any rock. You will see many tiny bits packed together in it. We call these bits minerals. A mineral is a solid. It does not live. It comes from the ground.

Each one has its own look. Some look very shiny, like metal. Others look dull and plain. Some are very hard. Others feel soft. One way to test hardness is to scratch it with a nail, a coin, or another mineral. A hard one resists a scratch. A soft one shows a mark right away.

Many of these bits grow into neat shapes called crystals. These shapes have flat sides that meet at sharp edges.

One very common kind is quartz. It is very hard and often clear, white, or pink. Another kind, halite, is better known as rock salt. People around the world eat it every day. A much softer kind called gypsum is used to make chalk and plaster.

People who dig in the desert find useful bits like salt, gold, and other rocks. These bits surround us every day, hidden inside many things we use at home.

versions.title: What Are Minerals?
versions.text:
Look closely at almost any rock. You will see many tiny bits packed tightly inside it. We call these bits minerals. A mineral is a natural, non-living solid found in the ground. It forms by nature, not by any plant, animal, or person.

Each one has its own look. This helps tell one apart from another. Some look very shiny, almost like metal. Others look dull and plain. Some feel very hard. Others feel soft and a bit crumbly. One way to test hardness is to scratch it with a nail, a coin, or another mineral. A hard one resists a scratch well. A soft one shows a mark right away.

Many of these bits grow into neat shapes called crystals. These shapes have flat sides that meet at sharp, straight edges in a pattern that repeats.

One very common kind is quartz. It is very hard and often clear, white, or pale pink. Another kind, halite, is better known as rock salt. People all around the world eat it every day as part of their food. A much softer kind called gypsum is used to make chalk, plaster, and other building materials.

People who dig in the desert find useful bits like salt, gold, and other rocks, and these bits help the country's economy. These bits surround us every day, hidden inside many things we use at home.

versions.title: Minerals: Building Blocks of Rocks
versions.text:
A single rock, however plain it may look, is usually not one substance. It is a mixture of several different minerals packed tightly together. Each mineral has its own makeup and its own crystal shape. Scientists have ways to identify them.

One key property is hardness. This tells how well a mineral resists a scratch. Scientists test hardness by trying to scratch a mineral with a nail, a coin, a knife, or another mineral, and they compare the marks. Another useful property is luster. This is how a mineral's surface reflects light. Some minerals have a bright, shiny luster. Others look glassy, pearly, or dull. A third helpful property is streak. This is the color of the powder a mineral leaves on a rough plate. Streak color can differ from the mineral's own surface color.

Quartz is one of the most common minerals on Earth. It is quite hard and usually clear, white, or pale pink. It is used in glass, watches, and phones. Halite, known as rock salt, dissolves easily in water. People use it daily in food. Gypsum, a much softer mineral, is ground up to make chalk, plaster, and drywall.

In the desert, miners dig up minerals such as phosphate, gold, and salt. Each one is used in a different way. By identifying the mixture of minerals in a rock, scientists can often tell how and where that rock formed.

versions.title: Minerals: Building Blocks of Rocks
versions.text:
A single rock, however plain it may look, is usually not one substance. It is a mixture of several minerals packed tightly together, each adding its own trait to the rock's overall composition. A mineral is a natural, non-living solid with its own chemical makeup and a crystalline structure, meaning its tiny parts repeat in an orderly pattern, and scientists classify minerals using a few simple, observable properties.

One key property is hardness, which tells how well a mineral resists a scratch from another object. In 1812, a scientist named Friedrich Mohs made a scale that ranks ten minerals from softest to hardest, with talc sitting at one and diamond, the hardest natural material, sitting at ten. Scientists still rely on this scale today, testing an unknown mineral by scratching it with reference minerals or simple objects like a nail or a knife.

Luster is another useful diagnostic clue, describing how a mineral's surface reflects light. Some minerals have a bright, metallic luster, while others look glassy, pearly, or dull. Streak is also helpful: it is the color of the powder a mineral leaves on a rough plate, and this color can differ from the mineral's own surface color, which helps tell similar-looking minerals apart.

Quartz has a crystalline structure that often forms sharp, six-sided points, and manufacturers use it in glass, watches, and electronics. Halite, or rock salt, dissolves easily in water, while gypsum, a much softer mineral, is ground into chalk, plaster, and drywall.

In the desert, miners dig up phosphate, gold, and salt, each supporting a different part of the economy. By classifying the mixture of minerals in a rock, scientists can often tell how and where that rock formed long ago. These same simple tests are still taught to students today, more than two hundred years after Mohs first devised them.

versions.title: Minerals: Building Blocks of Rocks
versions.text:
Nearly every rock encountered in nature is, strictly speaking, not a single substance but a composition of multiple minerals bound tightly together, and understanding those individual minerals reveals a great deal about the rock's origin. A mineral is formally defined as a naturally occurring, non-living solid with a specific chemical composition and a crystalline internal structure, meaning its atoms repeat in an orderly, predictable pattern throughout the material.

Geologists classify minerals using a handful of observable physical properties, the most famous being hardness. In 1812, the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs devised a simple ten-point scale that ranks reference minerals from softest to hardest: talc occupies the bottom of the scale at one, while diamond sits at the top at ten, prized partly because its exceptional hardness makes it useful for cutting tools as well as jewelry. Testing hardness in the field requires little more than a fingernail, a coin, a steel blade, and patience, since a mineral that scratches another is, by definition, the harder of the two.

Luster offers a second valuable clue. This property describes how a mineral's surface interacts with light, ranging from the bright sheen of metallic minerals to the softer glow of glassy, pearly, or waxy surfaces. Streak, meanwhile, examines the color of the powder a mineral produces when scraped across an unglazed ceramic plate, a test that can reveal a mineral's true identity even when its outward color has been altered by weathering or impurities.

Among the most familiar minerals is quartz, whose crystalline structure often grows into striking six-sided points and whose hardness makes it valuable in glass manufacturing, precision watches, and modern electronics. Halite, the mineral form of ordinary table salt, dissolves effortlessly in water, while gypsum, considerably softer than either quartz or halite, crumbles easily and has long been processed into plaster, chalk, and drywall.

Saudi Arabia's desert landscape conceals economically important mineral deposits, including phosphate used in fertilizer, gold extracted from historic mining regions, and salt harvested from dry desert flats, each contributing to a mineral sector that continues to expand as new surveys map the kingdom's subsurface resources.

Ultimately, learning to read a mineral's hardness, luster, streak, and crystalline form allows geologists to classify specimens accurately in the field, often without any laboratory equipment at all, turning a seemingly ordinary rock into a readable record of its own chemical composition and geological history. Students who practice these simple tests on a handful of common minerals often find that the skill transfers readily to rocks they encounter anywhere, from a schoolyard to a desert outcrop.

versions.title: Minerals: Building Blocks of Rocks
versions.text:
Nearly every rock encountered in nature is, strictly speaking, not a single homogeneous substance but rather a composition of multiple minerals bound tightly together, and understanding those individual constituent minerals reveals a considerable amount about the rock's broader origin and history. A mineral is formally defined as a naturally occurring, non-living solid possessing a specific chemical composition and a crystalline internal structure, meaning its constituent atoms repeat in an orderly, highly predictable pattern throughout the entire material.

Geologists classify minerals using a relatively small number of observable physical properties, the most famous among them being hardness. In 1812, the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs devised a deceptively simple ten-point scale that ranks ten reference minerals from softest to hardest: talc occupies the very bottom of the scale at one, while diamond sits at the top at ten, prized in part because its exceptional hardness makes it tremendously useful for industrial cutting tools as well as for jewelry. Testing hardness out in the field requires little more equipment than a fingernail, a coin, a steel blade, and a measure of patience, since a mineral capable of scratching another is, by strict definition, considered the harder of the two.

Luster offers geologists a second genuinely valuable diagnostic clue. This particular property describes precisely how a mineral's surface interacts with incoming light, ranging from the bright, unmistakable sheen of metallic minerals to the considerably softer glow of glassy, pearly, or waxy surfaces. Streak, meanwhile, examines the specific color of the fine powder a mineral produces when firmly scraped across an unglazed ceramic plate, a simple test that can reveal a mineral's true underlying identity even in cases where its outward surface color has been noticeably altered by weathering or by embedded impurities.

Among the most familiar and widely recognized minerals is quartz, whose distinctly crystalline structure frequently grows into striking six-sided points, and whose considerable hardness makes it genuinely valuable in glass manufacturing, precision watchmaking, and much of modern electronics. Halite, the mineral form of ordinary table salt, dissolves remarkably effortlessly in water, while gypsum, considerably softer than either quartz or halite, crumbles quite easily and has long been industrially processed into plaster, chalk, and drywall for widespread use in construction.

Saudi Arabia's extensive desert landscape conceals several economically important mineral deposits, including phosphate commonly used in fertilizer production, gold historically extracted from long-established mining regions, and salt regularly harvested from dry desert flats, each contributing meaningfully to a national mineral sector that continues to expand steadily as new geological surveys map the kingdom's subsurface resources in ever greater detail.

Ultimately, learning to carefully read a mineral's hardness, luster, streak, and crystalline form allows geologists to classify unfamiliar specimens with real accuracy out in the field, frequently without any laboratory equipment whatsoever, transforming what might initially seem like an entirely ordinary rock into a genuinely readable record of its own underlying chemical composition and deep geological history.

MID.prompt: Explain how hardness, luster, and streak each help scientists identify a mineral. Use at least three key words from the article.
checklist: I explained at least two identifying properties.
I used at least three key words correctly.
I included facts from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: Hardness helps scientists identify a mineral by showing how easily it can be scratched, since a hard mineral like quartz resists scratching while a soft one does not. Luster shows whether a mineral's surface looks metallic, glassy, or dull, and streak reveals the color of the powder a mineral leaves on a rough plate, which can differ from its surface color. Together, these properties help geologists identify the mixture of minerals inside any rock.

keyWords.definition: the particular substances or chemical elements that make up something
keyWords.example: The composition of seawater includes salt and other minerals.

keyWords.definition: having a structure made of orderly, repeating crystals
keyWords.example: Quartz has a crystalline structure that forms sharp, six-sided points.

keyWords.definition: to arrange or group things according to shared characteristics
keyWords.example: Scientists classify minerals by their hardness, color, and crystal shape.

keyWords.definition: a series of numbers or levels used to measure and compare something
keyWords.example: The Mohs scale ranks minerals from softest to hardest.

keyWords.definition: the way the parts of something are arranged and connected
keyWords.example: The internal structure of a crystal determines its shape.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how the Mohs scale and other properties allow geologists to classify minerals in the field without laboratory equipment. Support your explanation with evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained how the Mohs scale works.
I explained at least one other identifying property.
I supported my explanation with evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The Mohs scale, created by Friedrich Mohs in 1812, ranks minerals from softest, talc at one, to hardest, diamond at ten, and geologists use simple tools like a fingernail or coin to test where an unknown mineral falls on this scale. Combined with luster, which describes how a mineral's surface reflects light, and streak, the color of the powder a mineral leaves on a ceramic plate, this gives geologists several properties to compare. Because each property can be tested with everyday objects rather than laboratory equipment, geologists can classify a mineral's composition and crystalline structure directly out in the field.
